articles.title: DOJ drags Army into court standoff with explosive warning for red state: report
articles.description: DOJ told a federal appeals court the Army can detonate Iowa’s unstable lead explosives without an EPA permit, The Washington Sun reported on Friday. The Army planned to destroy 68 barrels of lead azide at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, the Sun wrote. After objections from Iowa and Illinois officials, it briefly delayed the plan, and environmental groups sued. The 8th Circuit paused the EPA’s emergency permit while it considers the case. In a Friday filing, a DOJ lawyer said an EPA rule lets the Army go ahead if it decides there is “an immediate threat to human health, public safety, property, or the environment,” according to the Sun. The Army isn’t a party to the suit. Army officials fear the aging explosive could go off by itself as it gets colder, the Sun reported, and the forecast shows temperatures falling Sunday and Monday nights. Acting Army Secretary Adam Telle said Monday was the last workable date before the drop. Iowa’s governor and many local communities said they heard about the plan only five days earlier, when the Army released maps showing lead dust could spread far from the plant, the paper wrote. The news of the planned detonation has triggered widespread fear throughout the region. Earthjustice attorney Thien Chau, who represents the plaintiffs, called the rule a last resort for cases with no other option. He asked the Army not to use it to avoid the transparency and protections people were demanding, the Sun reported. The Army, EPA, and Health and Human Services issued a joint statement Friday that didn’t mention the court order. It said officials had planned since March and were ready with strong safety measures, the Sun wrote. DOJ said it would respond to plaintiffs' emergency motion for a stay before Monday, the Sun reported.
